Reframed with literature-based context: The FOMC’s September 2020 statement pairs a state-contingent zero-rate commitment with continued Treasury and agency MBS purchases, aligning with New Keynesian guidance that credible forward-looking rules help stabilize output and inflation (e.g., Taylor-rule style guidelines and Clarida–Gali–Gertler). The shift to average inflation targeting—explicitly allowing inflation to run moderately above 2 percent—addresses time-inconsistency concerns by anchoring expectations around the target over time while lowering real rates at the effective lower bound via expectations management. Asset purchases and reinvestments are consistent with evidence that the Fed can influence the slope of the yield curve and financial conditions (as emphasized in work studied by the Fed, including Piazzesi), while the emphasis on smooth market functioning, repos, and ON RRP reflects the operational literature in which money-market operations transmit policy to funding markets. The statement’s recognition of COVID-related demand weakness and low oil prices as disinflationary is consistent with standard models where adverse shocks push inflation below target; the commitment to continued accommodation aims to offset these forces and support credit flow, consistent with the credit-channel literature (Bernanke and coauthors). The dissents map to longstanding debates: one favoring more flexibility in the reaction function (to avoid policy inertia) and the other favoring a stricter commitment until core inflation sustainably reaches 2 percent (to ensure expectations re-anchor), paralleling discussions of rule credibility versus discretion (e.g., Orphanides’ work on misperceptions and the 1970s experience).

Net tone: still cautious due to “considerable risks” and expected near-term drag, but somewhat less negative than a purely backward-looking read, given the literature-backed efficacy of commitment and balance-sheet policies in easing financial conditions and anchoring expectations.
